svg.aria-label: Diagram: what an Amazon SQS queue's signals actually report, and where the consumer's drain rate is decided. On the left, the three queue metrics and what each one answers. ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible is the accumulated backlog, an integral of arrival minus completion, so it reports that you are behind but never why, and AWS notes a consistently high value may mean under-provisioned consumers or stuck processing logic. ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage appears to report latency but excludes failing work: AWS states that a standard-queue message received three or more times and not deleted is moved to the back of the queue, the metric then reports the next message that has not exceeded the receive threshold, this happens even with a redrive policy in place, and poison-pill messages are excluded from the metric until successfully processed, so the metric improves as messages become stuck. ApproximateNumberOfMessagesNotVisible counts in-flight messages but may rarely report non-zero on an empty queue, so AWS advises evaluating several consecutive data points. On the right, the drain rate: a default Lambda event source mapping begins at five concurrent invocations, increases by up to 300 more concurrent invokes per minute driven by the backlog itself rather than by any human decision, and stops at a ceiling of 1,250 simultaneous invokes. The maximum concurrency setting, accepting a value between 2 and 1,000, is the valve that caps this deliberately, and provisioned mode instead scales up to 1,000 concurrency per minute toward as many as 100,000 concurrent invokes. A panel at the bottom records the consequence: the queue defers load rather than absorbing it, so raising the drain rate delivers the deferred load to whatever the consumers depend on, and the drain rate should be sized to the slowest dependency downstream rather than to the depth of the queue.
svg.title: Three signals answering three different questions, and a drain rate that rises on its own
svg.text: The queue reports less than the dashboard implies
A queue defers load; it never makes the work smaller. Draining faster only decides when it arrives.
What each signal actually answers
ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible
The accumulated backlog — arrival minus completion, integrated.
Tells you that you are behind. Never why.
ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage
“received three or more times and not deleted” → moved to the
back of the queue. The metric reports the next message instead.
Poison pills “excluded from this metric until successfully processed.”
It gets healthier as messages get stuck.
ApproximateNumberOfMessagesNotVisible
In flight — but may read non-zero on an empty queue.
Alarm on consecutive datapoints, never a single one.
Where the drain rate is decided
Default event source mapping
start 5
Driven by the backlog itself. Nobody scales anything.
Scales back to 5, and to as few as 2 when quiet —
but not once maximum concurrency is enabled.
The valve: maximum concurrency, 2 to 1,000.
Provisioned mode instead: up to 100,000 concurrent invokes.
Two settings that look like one
Maximum concurrency above reserved concurrency does not
raise the ceiling — it throttles, which becomes retries.
What draining faster actually does
The queue deferred the load. Raising the drain rate delivers it — concentrated — to whatever the consumers depend on:
a database, a third-party API, a service with its own limits and no view of your queue.
Size the drain rate to the slowest dependency downstream, not to the depth of the queue.
Read the metric definitions, not the metric names. The one that sounds like it would reveal a stuck message is the one documented not to.
Stuck work becomes visible at the DLQ — by its visible-message count, since redriven arrivals never appear in NumberOfMessagesSent.
